tagline.text: A cave journey to the origins of the Filipino people

children.text: A prehistoric site where more than 200 caves cluster on a limestone headland in Quezon, southwestern Palawan — the "Cradle of Philippine Civilization," where the Philippines' oldest modern human fossils, Tabon Man, and the national treasure Manunggul Jar were unearthed. A coastal boardwalk leads you through the caves and the on-site museum.

Tabon Caves is an archaeological cave site at Lipuun Point, in the village of Panitian, Quezon, on the southwestern coast of the Palawan mainland. About 218 caves are scattered across the entire limestone headland jutting into the sea, and around 38 of them have yielded human bones, pottery, stone tools, and ornaments. The Philippines' National Museum manages the site directly, and Filipinos call it the "Cradle of Philippine Civilization."
On
, an excavation team led by American anthropologist Robert Fox found skull fragments of a young woman in the main cave. Known as "Tabon Man," this fossil dates to about
16,500 years ago
, making it one of the oldest modern human remains found in the Philippines. A shinbone fragment found afterward dates back as far as about
47,000 years ago
, and traces show the caves were almost continuously inhabited from 30,000 to 9,000 years ago.
In later periods the caves were used as burial sites, yielding more than 1,500 burial jars. The most famous, the Manunggul Jar, was made around

and carved on its lid with two figures rowing a boat that carries a soul to the afterlife. The original is a National Cultural Treasure held at the National Museum of Anthropology in Manila, while replicas and the story of the excavation can be seen at the on-site museum here. The cave complex was added to UNESCO's World Heritage Tentative List in
When the on-site museum opened at Lipuun Point in
February 2024

and a concrete path and boardwalk were laid along the coast, it became possible to walk all the way to the cave entrances without hiring a boat as before. You may be disappointed if you're expecting a cave dripping with dramatic stalactites, but standing in a spot where people lived tens of thousands of years ago is a special experience. Recommended for travelers interested in history and archaeology, and for anyone touring less-visited southern Palawan.

Four exhibit halls introduce Tabon Man's skull, a replica of the Manunggul Jar, the begonias and ferns that grow only in the caves, and the indigenous Palawan people's knowledge of the stars. Seeing this before entering the caves makes everything much easier to follow.
A concrete path and boardwalk run about
1.3km
between mangroves and limestone cliffs to the cave entrances, with views of a clear-watered bay and cliffs unfolding together along the way.

The largest cave, where the Tabon Man fossil was found — excavation markers still stand inside the wide entrance. Light streaming through a hole in the ceiling keeps the cave brighter than you'd expect.

With a guide, work your way through several other open caves such as Diwata Cave and Igang Cave. Each cave held burial jars in a different spot and served a different purpose, so the guide's explanation is essential.

blocks.title: The story of the Manunggul Jar

children.text: Listen to the story of Manunggul Cave, where the burial jar reflecting the ancient Filipinos' view of the afterlife was found. Seeing the original at the National Museum in Manila completes the experience.
A small island off the coast of Quezon, where a white sandbar nearly 1km long appears at low tide. It's a good idea to rent a banca and combine it with the beach on Sidnayan Island.
A waterfall in the forest outside Quezon, reached with a short trek and a river boat ride — a nice way to cool off in the afternoon after seeing the caves.

Arrive in Puerto Princesa
If you're short on time, you can also charter a vehicle from Puerto Princesa for a pre-dawn day trip, but since that means spending 7–8 hours in the car round-trip, an overnight stay is recommended.
Manila to Puerto Princesa International Airport (PPS) takes about
1 hour 20 minutes
, with one-way fares around
. Quezon has no airport, so you continue overland from here.
Cherry Bus and other operators, along with shared vans, depart for Quezon from San Jose Terminal north of Puerto Princesa, passing through Narra town — about
150km
, taking
3–4 hours
. Fares run around
Departures aren't frequent and services stop running by late afternoon, so leave in the morning, and confirm your return departure time at the terminal in advance.
Chartering a van with a driver from Puerto Princesa costs about
per vehicle, which is worthwhile for a day trip if there are four or more of you. Most of the southern coastal road is paved.
First, stop by the National Museum office in Quezon town's Alfonso XIII village to register your visit. From there, you charter a tricycle to Lipuun Point for a round trip costing around
In the past, visitors rented a banca from the pier and crossed about
30 minutes–1 hour
of open water, and this banca route, combined with island hopping, is still an option today. Chartering a banca costs about
per boat.
November
through
May

is the dry season and the best time to visit. During this period the western sea is relatively calm, making it a good time to combine island hopping, and the boardwalk and cave floors are less slippery. In
March–May
, midday temperatures climb to around
, so it's best to explore the caves early in the morning or late in the afternoon.
From
June
to
October

, the southwest monsoon blows directly onto the west coast where Quezon sits, bringing frequent rain and high waves. The caves themselves are reachable on foot, but island-hopping boats are often canceled, and the cave floors turn muddy after heavy rain. If you visit during this period, a short itinerary focused on just the caves and museum is more realistic.

Quezon is a small farming and fishing town without many tourists, so lodging is simple. Around the town center and pier are pensions and lodges running about
a night, and outside town along the coast are a few small beach resorts at about

a night. Many places don't take online bookings, so it's more reliable to contact them ahead by phone or Facebook message. If amenities matter to you, visiting on a day trip from Puerto Princesa is another option.

Food centers on home-style cooking at carinderias around the market. At the pier you can eat the day's catch of fish, squid, and crab grilled or in sinigang, and you can also try chaolong, the Vietnamese-style rice noodle soup enjoyed all over Palawan, for about
a bowl. Restaurants close early, so plan dinner around sunset, and bring plenty of water and snacks on cave-exploring days.

National Museum facilities are often closed on Mondays. Before visiting, it's best to check opening days and registration procedures through the National Museum Tabon Cave Complex's Facebook page or by phone.
Cave visits are meant to be done with a guide after registering. Without the commentary, the caves can look like empty holes, so be sure to listen to your guide's stories.
There are stairs and slopes between the boardwalk and the caves, so wear non-slip sneakers or aqua shoes.
Some stretches inside the caves are dark, so a small flashlight or headlamp is handy.
Quezon has few ATMs and card payment is rarely accepted, so bring cash from Puerto Princesa.
Seeing the original Manunggul Jar and Tabon Man skull at the National Museum of Anthropology in Manila, before or after your trip, ties the story together and makes it much more interesting.
If you're combining this with a southern Palawan trip, it's efficient to continue south from Quezon toward Brooke's Point and Rio Tuba.

Tabon Cave Complex is an excavation site protected as a National Cultural Treasure. Touching or removing soil, stones, bones, or pottery fragments from the caves is prohibited by law, and access rules can change per National Museum notices, so check the latest guidance.
Don't cross the excavation markers and ropes, and don't write on or lean against the cave walls.
Cave floors are slippery with bat droppings and moisture. Move slowly to avoid falling, and it's a good idea to bring hand sanitizer.
Some forested parts of southern Palawan still carry a malaria risk, so bring long sleeves and mosquito repellent.
During the rainy season, high waves can lead to sudden banca cancellations. If the coast guard halts departures, follow their orders.
Public transport between Quezon and Puerto Princesa stops running in the afternoon, so build in enough time in your schedule to catch your ride back.
